legacy_report:
SOURCE: "@skills: Attention Is All You Have. An open agent skills protocol, built for the future of knowledge sharing." Li Yin, Zhi Li, Zhan Shi, Haoran Zhang, Haebin Seong (SylphAI), Zhangyang (Atlas) Wang (UT Austin). arXiv:2608.12610v1 [cs.AI], 12 Aug 2026, marked "A PREPRINT". No peer-reviewed venue.

COVERAGE: 122,688 of 122,689 chars read (full text, 26 pages incl. appendices A-H). The reference pages (8-10) were skimmed, not read closely. No extraction faults. Figures were not rendered, only their captions in the text. Extraction offsets below are page numbers.

ASSESSMENT (plain): This is a design and advocacy paper, not an empirical one. The central quantity, "fewer than 100 reliable auto-trigger slots", is argued from other papers and not measured. The authors say so. The author founded SylphAI, which sells the AdaL agent and the hub the paper promotes. It is relevant to context engineering only for its framing (resident context is a budget; deliver at the point of use; progressive disclosure across an ecosystem). Its protocol details (@skills, .atskills/, .autotrigger) are product-specific. It does not belong in 09-protocols.md as a protocol on a par with MCP. At most it earns a pointer as a skills-delivery proposal. It fits 04-retrieval's Just-in-time section better.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Main thesis: installing a skill bundles content, persistence and auto-triggering, and only auto-triggering needs prompt residency. The paper proposes making the other two free.
  number: none
  setup: design argument, no experiment
  quote: "Our observation is that installing bundles three separable functions—content, persistence, and auto-triggering—and only the last needs the prompt."
  where: p1 abstract
- Principle that generalizes (the most quotable line for the notes).
  number: none
  quote: "resident context is a budget; spend it only on what must fire implicitly, and deliver everything else at the point of use, where attention is highest."
  where: p7 (Sec. 4)
- Scale mismatch: 56,804 skills compete for a small trigger budget.
  number: 56,804 SKILL.md directories in 1,133 public GitHub repos; budget "fewer than 100"
  setup: July 2026 crawl of the skills.sh index. 56,245 bodies (99%) were fetched. It is an upper bound on unique skills because duplicates are not removed.
  quote: "56,804 indexed skills compete for fewer than 100 reliable auto-trigger slots per agent."
  where: p3, p16
- The slot cap is a bound inferred from the literature, not measured.
  number: "<100"
  quote: "We do not claim a precise constant; no controlled measurement of trigger reliability versus installed-skill count yet exists"
  where: p14-15 (App. C.1)
  Also, on p7: "bounded by argument and by the literature rather than measured by us".
- Standing token tax of resident descriptions.
  number: 50-280 tokens per skill; 18 installed skills is about 1,500-2,000 tokens on every request. Under @skills the frontmatter of an installed skill is about 50-100 tokens.
  setup: "one real working setup", not a survey
  quote: "we find 50–280 tokens per skill; that session, with 18 installed skills, carries roughly 1,500–2,000 tokens of standing overhead on every request."
  where: p14
- Trigger-engineered descriptions cost about 20x more tokens. Stripe's flagship skill carries about 150 words of them.
  number: ~20x; ~150 words
  setup: "among the examples we examined"; full-corpus prevalence is not measured
  quote: "TRIGGER-block descriptions cost roughly 20× more tokens than quiet ones"
  where: p15
- Skill bodies are too big to keep resident but cheap to fetch.
  number: median 921 words, p90 2,207, mean 1,159 (about 1.2k-3.7k tokens at the median)
  setup: 56,245 fetched bodies. The token range assumes 1.3-4 tokens per word.
  quote: "The median fetched skill body is 921 words and the 90th percentile is 2,207 (mean 1,159)"
  where: p12
- Corpus facts. Both samples are small, and the paper itself marks them as weak.
  numbers: 21 provider orgs publish 958 first-party skills. Of 569 skills in fifteen provider repos, 79% name the provider's CLI or API and 60% contain shell blocks. Category shares (30% software engineering, 25% creative, 16% writing, 15% design) come from a 100-skill sample with about ±10 points at 95% confidence. The top 15 repos hold 51% of skills.
  quote: "classification figures ... come from a 100-skill uniform sample carrying roughly ±10 percentage points at 95% confidence."
  where: p12-13
  The shell-block figure is flagged as an upper bound by substring matching (footnote 2).
- Fragmentation: 75 agents use 54 project-level skill directories and 58 user-level locations.
  quote: "It supports 75 coding agents using 54 distinct project-level skills directories."
  where: p13
- Three tiers: Reference (@skills:path, 0 resident tokens, explicit); Saved (.atskills/, git-tracked, 10-30 skills, 0 resident tokens, indexed by tooling and not by the prompt); Installed (.autotrigger, fewer than 10, frontmatter resident).
  quote: "we recommend fewer than ten essentials, since every addition dilutes the rest."
  where: p16
  Tier 2 is pitched as AGENTS.md "factored into pieces".
- Mechanism claim: position, not semantics, is the cause. An explicit reference injects the full SKILL.md at the end of context, next to the task.
  number: none from the authors' own tests; relies on cited work: 39% average loss in long multi-turn vs single-turn [8]; 68% adherence at 500 concurrent constraints for the best frontier model [12]
  quote: "models in long multi-turn settings lose an average of 39% against single-turn performance on the same tasks [8]"
  where: p14
  The paper concedes the 500-constraint experiment "measures concurrent constraints rather than trigger descriptions, so we take it as suggestive rather than direct".
- MCP context cost, taken from Anthropic's blog and not measured here.
  number: 150,000 to 2,000 tokens (98.7%); GitHub's official MCP server has about 93 tool definitions
  quote: "reporting a drop from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens (98.7%) on an equivalent task"
  where: p10
  Also, "1,899 open-source MCP servers, 66% exhibited code smells and 5.5% shipped tool-poisoning vulnerabilities [25]".
- Explicit versus retrieval-based triggering (for 04-retrieval). RAG retrieval is implicit and similarity-based. @skills is explicit and deterministic. The authors call retrieval-based triggering complementary and future work, since it brings back probabilistic activation.
  quote: "RAG retrieval is implicit and similarity-based; @skills references are explicit and deterministic, which is what reliability requires for instructions as opposed to facts."
  where: p26
- Explicit references make multi-skill workflows deterministic, where installed skills must each win a probabilistic match (asserted, not tested).
  where: p4
- Link to the Just-in-time section. The paper cites Anthropic [39], "Effective context engineering", and adds one step.
  quote: "Tiers 1 and 2 are just-in-time retrieval, with the piece the guidance lacks: an ecosystem-wide protocol and catalog behind the fetch"
  where: p17
- Progressive disclosure inside a skill: "metadata stays resident, the body loads on relevance, and bundled files load on demand [3]". This paper extends it to delivery across the ecosystem.
  where: p11
- Design details useful for a protocols note. Protocol facts, not evidence.
  - Path is identity. A directory loads as a menu, one line per skill (leaf rule).
  - Resolution is local-first, then a validating cache at ~/.cache/atskills. Each use costs one `git ls-remote` revision probe.
  - Collection cap K=128 skills (App. F).
  - :save vendors a copy and writes a two-line .source stamp. There is no pinning and no update lifecycle.
  - :install adds one gitignore-style line to .autotrigger.
  - Two ownership states only: "theirs" (followed) and "yours" (saved).
  - Fetched skills are remote text the agent follows, the indirect-prompt-injection channel. The authors rely on provenance and review, not filtering.
  - The protocol is "implemented in AdaL" (their product). No third-party adoption is shown.

LIMITS (authors' own and mine)
- No controlled experiment on trigger reliability against installed-skill count, or on compliance against injection position. Both are listed as future work.
- Token measurements come from one working setup. Corpus numbers come from one crawl.
- Quote: "If future architectures or harness-side calibration reduce positional bias, the residency argument weakens, though the standing-tax, dilution, and lifecycle arguments do not."
- Quote: "A referenced skill also drifts from the task in very long sessions". Tier 1 puts a network round trip on the critical path.
- Conflict of interest, quoted: "The author founded SylphAI, which develops AdaL and operates the catalog and hub described here, so this paper advocates infrastructure its author runs."
- Security is not solved: "The risk is not new ... but it is not removed either." Typosquatting and name confusion are acknowledged.
- The retrieval-based alternative is not built or compared.
- The "AGENTS.md won because of simplicity" claim is admitted to be unprovable: "We cannot tell teams that defected from skills apart from teams whose AGENTS.md practice simply came first".
- The 56,804 count is an upper bound, with duplicates only partly removed.
- Dated: ecosystem numbers are as of July 2026.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Anthropic, Agent Skills and the engineering blog "Equipping agents for the real world with agent skills" (2025), for the format and progressive disclosure [2,3].
- Anthropic, MCP (2024) [4].
- Anthropic context-engineering guidance [39], for just-in-time retrieval.
- Simon Willison, "Claude skills are awesome" (2025) [5].
- Vercel skills.sh [1], the closest neighbour (its `use` command).
- Liu et al. [6] ("lost in the middle") plus [36, 37] for positional bias.
- [7] system-message decay; [8] 39% multi-turn loss; [9] length alone degrades reasoning; [10] effective context smaller than advertised; [11] distraction; [12] 500-constraint instruction following.
- RAG [47,48]; Rubin et al. [49]; Self-RAG [50].
- Weng [51]; Voyager, Reflexion, ExpeL, Agent Workflow Memory [52-55] (AWM: +24-51% relative on web tasks).
- Gorilla, ToolLLM [58,59]; MemGPT [63]; Karpathy's LLM-as-OS framing [62].
- Go vendor/ and npm per-project dependencies, as the packaging precedent.

CODE (verbatim, App. E.1, p18; the .autotrigger format is on p20)
```
@skills:gh:stripe/agent-toolkit    a directory -> a menu, one line per skill
@skills:<path>:save                copy into the project -- to adapt it
@skills:<path>:install             append its line to .autotrigger
@skills:<path>:save:install        both -- your copy, firing on its own
```
```
# .atskills/.autotrigger
sec-checklist                    yours -- lives in .atskills/, reviewed
team-flows/                      yours -- every skill under the directory
@hub:sylphai/glowmotion          hub -- follows the author's latest
@gh:stripe/agent-toolkit/payments  github -- follows Stripe's latest
```

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p2): the three delivery tiers with their token costs. It explains the budget logic faster than prose.
- Fig. 2 (p3): a 2x2 of "fires without being asked" against "own a copy", showing that :save and :install are orthogonal.
- Fig. 5 (p14): install-only (description at the top of context, decaying) against reference delivery (full body injected adjacent to the task). It is the best single picture of the positional argument. It is schematic, not data.
- Fig. 4 (p12): how installed skills work today (description resident, body loaded on trigger).
- Fig. 3 (p6): the whole protocol in one look, with the /skills screen showing "190 tok".

PROBLEMS: none in extraction. No embedded instructions found. References were skimmed only. Do not cite the 100-slot figure as a measured result. Do not cite the corpus-classification percentages without the ±10 point caveat.
